opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it comes from watching what happened with the community over the last year or so. When we started LeRobot, the idea was to do for robotics what we'd tried to do for NLP: open models, open datasets, open tooling, so that anyone could get started without needing a huge lab behind them. And the software side moved really fast. People were training policies, sharing datasets on the Hub, reproducing results. That part worked.

But we kept hitting the same wall, which is hardware. Software is something you can just download. A robot you have to source parts for, 3D print, assemble, calibrate, debug the motors. The open-source arms were amazing for the people willing to do that, and we love that maker crowd; they're the heart of the community. But for every person who built one, there were probably ten who were curious and gave up at the "order the servos from three different websites" step.

So the thinking is: if you want robotics to become something like what the transformer moment was for language, you need a lot more people experimenting. Students, hobbyists, researchers in labs that don't have a robotics budget, developers who just want to play with AI in the physical world. And for that, the hardware has to be something you can unbox and use. Affordable, reliable, looks good on a desk, works with the open software stack out of the box.

There's also a data angle, which I think people underestimate. Robotics is fundamentally data-starved. We don't have an internet of robot actions the way we had an internet of text. If you can get thousands of fairly standardized, polished devices out there, all connected to an open ecosystem, you suddenly have a path to community-scale data collection. That's the kind of thing that could unlock much better models.

And finally, it's about keeping things open. If the only good robots end up being closed platforms from a handful of big companies, we lose what made AI progress so fast in the first place. Having open hardware that's also genuinely nice to use is how you make open the default rather than the niche option.

r001.rationale: The response says polished, ready-to-use hardware would let students, researchers, and developers participate, extending access beyond the maker crowd willing to source and assemble parts.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that robotics today feels a lot like NLP did back in 2018, before we built Transformers and the Hub. Everything was fragmented. Every lab had its own robot, its own data format, its own training loop, and nothing was really reproducible. If you wanted to replicate a paper, you basically had to rebuild the hardware yourself, which is kind of insane.

So when we started LeRobot, the idea was: let's make the software side open and standardized, the same way we did for models and datasets. But very quickly you realize that in robotics, software alone isn't enough. The data comes from the physical world, and if the community can't get its hands on a physical system that's affordable and actually works, you only have maybe a few hundred people worldwide who can contribute. That's not a community, that's a club.

That's why we did things like the SO-100 and SO-101 arms, which are very low cost, a few hundred dollars, you can 3D print parts and assemble them yourself. And the response was amazing, way more than we expected. But we also saw the friction. People spend a weekend assembling the arm, calibrating the servos, fighting with the wiring, and some of them give up before they ever collect a single dataset. And honestly, I feel that too, I'm not a hardware person by background.

So the goal of pushing toward more polished, mass-market hardware, and that's also part of why we did the Pollen Robotics acquisition with Reachy, is really about lowering the entry barrier. I want a student, or a developer who's never touched a robot, to be able to unbox something, plug it in, and within an hour be teleoperating it, recording episodes, and uploading them to the Hub. When that happens at scale, you start getting the thing that made language models work, which is massive, diverse, shared data. Nobody is going to solve robotics with a single lab's dataset. It has to be thousands of people, with thousands of robots, in thousands of kitchens and garages.

And there's a second reason, which is more philosophical. I think it matters a lot who ends up controlling robotics. If the only polished, well-integrated robots come from two or three closed companies, then the whole field becomes a black box, the same risk we saw with closed models. We'd like there to be an open alternative that's not just a research toy, something that's genuinely nice to use, that a company could actually build a product on. Open source wins when it's good, not just when it's free. So making the hardware polished isn't a nice-to-have, it's really the condition for the open ecosystem to be competitive at all.

r001.rationale: The response says polished hardware should let students and developers with no robotics experience get started quickly, lowering the entry barrier beyond experienced hobbyists.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to make it much easier for people to get started. If you want to explore robotics, you can spend a lot of your time just getting the hardware to work. That can be interesting, but it’s also a barrier if what you really want to do is teach a robot something.

More polished hardware lets more people participate. You don’t have to be a robotics engineer to try an idea, collect some demonstrations, or share what you’ve learned. And having a common platform makes that sharing much more useful: something that works for me has a better chance of working for you.

That’s what I’d like to bring to LeRobot—a shorter path from being curious about robotics to actually contributing. The hardware is a way to open up that experimentation to a much larger community.

r001.rationale: The response says polished hardware lets more people participate without being robotics engineers and opens experimentation to a much larger community, clearly conveying appeal beyond the existing hobbyist audience.

sol-6.1.text:
Because we want more people to be able to experiment with robotics. Today, even getting a robot set up can take a lot of time and expertise before you can start working on the learning side. More polished hardware lowers that barrier. You can get it, switch it on, and start collecting data or trying a model.

And having a lot of people use the same hardware makes sharing much more useful. If I collect a dataset or train a policy, you can try it on your robot too. That’s the kind of collaboration we want to make easier with LeRobot.

r001.rationale: The response says polished hardware will let more people experiment by lowering setup barriers, but it does not clearly identify broadening appeal beyond hobbyists and hackers as the goal.
